subject.name: Religious Education

units.name: Judaism: Beliefs and Teachings
units.subtitle: God, the Covenant, the mitzvot and the sanctity of life

units.name: Judaism: Practices
units.subtitle: The synagogue, Shabbat, family rituals and festivals

common_misconceptions.topic: Anatta vs the Western 'no soul' framing
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students translate anatta as 'there is no soul' and stop. The Buddhist teaching is more precise: there is no fixed, permanent, unchanging self — the personality is the Five Aggregates (skandhas) in flux. Mark schemes reward the technical phrasing.

Students confuse atman (the eternal inner self of an individual) with Brahman (ultimate reality). Some Hindu schools (Advaita Vedanta) hold that atman IS Brahman; others distinguish them. Top-band answers name a sub-tradition (Shaivism, Vaishnavism, Advaita).

common_misconceptions.topic: Kamma / karma as fate vs as moral causation
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat kamma (Buddhism) and karma (Hinduism, Sikhism) as 'fate' or 'destiny'. The teaching across traditions is moral causation: intentional actions produce consequences across this life and into rebirth. There is room for free will and skilful action to alter the trajectory.

common_misconceptions.topic: Mitzvot as restrictive rules vs as joyful duties
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students describe the 613 mitzvot as 'rules Jews have to follow'. Jewish teaching frames mitzvot as commandments (between man and God, and between man and man) that bring sanctity to daily life. Pikuach Nefesh — saving a life — overrides nearly all of them, showing the priority of life and human dignity.

common_misconceptions.topic: Sewa as charity vs as worship
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students describe sewa as 'helping others' alone. Sikh teaching frames sewa as worship — physical (tan), mental (man) and material (dhan) service expressed in langar and at the gurdwara. Reducing it to 'volunteering' loses the religious depth.

common_misconceptions.topic: Trinity as 'three gods' vs one God in three persons
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students describe the Trinity as 'Christians believe in three gods'. Catholic and broader Christian teaching is one God in three persons — Father, Son, Holy Spirit — articulated in the Nicene Creed at Nicaea (325). The technical phrase 'one God, three persons' or 'one substance, three persons' wins marks.

Students give arguments for and arguments against and stop. AQA's 12-mark mark scheme requires a JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION — a reasoned judgement of which side is stronger and WHY. Without that final paragraph, the answer caps mid-band.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA 8062 sample assessment material mark schemes (2018-2024).

common_misconceptions.topic: The 6-mark Explain without a source of authority
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students forget the 6-mark Explain question's 'must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching' instruction. Without naming a source — Genesis 1, the Mool Mantra (GGS 1a), Dhammapada 190-191, the Shema, the Lord's Prayer, the Sermon on the Mount — the response caps below the top band.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA 8062 sample assessment material mark schemes (2018-2024).

common_misconceptions.topic: Same-sex relationships — treating Christianity as a single voice
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students write 'Christianity teaches X about same-sex relationships' as if there is one position. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Methodist, evangelical Protestant and Quaker positions vary widely. Theme F mark schemes reward CONTRASTING views (within Christianity AND with non-religious views).

common_misconceptions.topic: Status of women — treating Judaism / Islam / Hinduism as monolithic
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students write 'Judaism teaches that women should...' without distinguishing Orthodox, Reform and Liberal positions. Same in Hinduism (where ancient text and contemporary practice differ widely) and Sikhism (where the spec emphasises COMPLETE equality). Top-band Theme F answers always name the sub-tradition.

student_errors_by_question_type.1 mark — Multiple Choice: Candidates leave items blank rather than committing. AQA RS 1-mark items use 'Which one of the following...' wording; pick the best of four. Even an educated guess is worth a mark.
student_errors_by_question_type.1 mark — Identify / Name: Candidates write a sentence when one term is required. 'Name a Sikh festival' wants 'Vaisakhi', not a sentence about Vaisakhi.
student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — State / Give: Candidates give one developed point when 2 marks usually rewards two distinct items. Use the structure: point 1 + point 2 (e.g. 'Two Buddhist festivals are Wesak and Parinirvana Day').
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Explain: Candidates list facts instead of giving reasons or contrasting beliefs. The 'Give two contrasting beliefs' or 'Give two ways' prompt rewards two distinct points each developed once. Use 'because' or 'this means that' on each.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Explain (Extended Response): Candidates forget the source-of-authority requirement. The mark scheme says 'In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.' Always name a source (Genesis 1, the Mool Mantra GGS 1a, Dhammapada 190-191, the Sermon on the Mount, the Five Pillars) AND develop two reasons.
student_errors_by_question_type.8 marks — Discuss / Analyse (Extended Re: Rare on AQA RS but registered for completeness. Candidates give one side of an argument and stop. Discuss / Analyse requires multiple perspectives weighed, including sub-tradition contrasts and non-religious views where relevant.
student_errors_by_question_type.12 marks — Evaluate (Extended Response): Candidates describe rather than evaluate, or give arguments for and against without reaching a conclusion. Top-band answers state the statement, give arguments FOR it (with religious sources), give arguments AGAINST (with religious sources and non-religious where relevant), and reach a JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION saying which side is stronger and why. SPaG marks also assessed on these.

topic_weighting_notes: Component 1 is 96 marks across 1 hour 45 minutes for two religions (each marked out of 48). Plus 6 SPaG marks. 50% of qualification.
Component 2 is 96 marks for four themes (each marked out of 24). Plus 3 SPaG marks. 50% of qualification.

Each religion has TWO five-part questions of 1, 1, 4, 6, 12 marks. Each theme has ONE five-part question of 1, 1, 4, 6, 12 marks. The structure is highly predictable — students who drill the question shapes capture 30-40% of the marks on form alone.
Assessment objective weighting: AO1 (knowledge) 50% and AO2 (analyse / evaluate) 50%. There is NO AO3 on AQA RS — never write AO3 anywhere.
Beliefs and Practices are weighted equally within each religion. Themes are weighted equally with each other.

Highest extended-response cap is 12 marks (Evaluate). 6-mark and 12-mark levels-based extended responses appear at every religion and every theme. Use StudyVault rubric (Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging) for both.

Sub-tradition contrasts (Theravada / Mahayana, Catholic / Orthodox / Protestant, Shaivism / Vaishnavism, Orthodox / Reform / Liberal Judaism, sahajdhari / amritdhari) are EXPECTED in top-band answers. Mark schemes explicitly reward 'recognise diversity within a religion'.
current_spec_changes: Specification version is 1.3 (1 September 2025). The amendments are administrative (assessment opportunities, codes) — no change to examinable subject content since first teaching in 2016.
First teaching from 2016, first award from 2018. Linear qualification, summer assessment series only.

Two routes: (a) non-Textual studies (two religions + four themes from A-F) — this gap-fill build supports route (a). (b) Textual studies (one of Christianity / Catholic + one other religion + two themes A-F + Themes G and H from St Mark's Gospel) — Themes G and H are NOT in this gap-fill build.
pedagogical_notes: EEF Metacognition (effect size +8 months) — explicitly model the 12-mark Evaluate structure: state the statement, arguments FOR with religious sources, arguments AGAINST with religious sources and non-religious views where relevant, justified conclusion. Walk through one worked example before students attempt independently.

EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools — disciplinary literacy is critical in RE. Students must use precise religious vocabulary in the tradition's own language: anicca, anatta, dukkha (NOT 'impermanence, no-self, suffering' as their first reach); kosher / trefah (NOT 'allowed / not allowed'); mitzvot, Pikuach Nefesh, sewa, mukti, gurmukh, dharma, atman, Brahman, sangat. Teach the term first, then unpack it.

Retrieval practice — the spec is dense with named lists (Three Marks of Existence; Five Aggregates; Three Poisons; Four Noble Truths; Eightfold Path; Five Moral Precepts; Six Perfections; seven sacraments; Trinity; three features of the divine in Hinduism; Tri-murti; four aims of life; four yogas; 613 mitzvot categories; Ten Commandments; five khands; five Ks). Short, frequent low-stakes retrieval quizzes outperform single long revision sessions for this content. Each lesson ends with a 5-question knowledge check.

Worked examples for the 6-mark Explain — model how to structure: opener naming the topic; reason 1 with development and source citation (e.g. Genesis 1:27); reason 2 with development and source. Students do not chain reasoning automatically.

Concrete real-world examples in every abstract concept. Brahman becomes more graspable when paired with the Diwali rangoli outside a mandir in Leicester. Pikuach Nefesh becomes vivid in the example of a Reform synagogue in Manchester delivering soup to vulnerable elderly people on Shabbat. Tie abstract teachings to British religious life today.

Sub-tradition contrast as a recall hook — pair every belief with a contrast. 'Theravada Buddhists stress the Arhat ideal; Mahayana Buddhists stress the Bodhisattva ideal.' 'Orthodox Jewish synagogues separate men and women; Reform synagogues are mixed.' This dual-coding helps retrieval AND mark-scheme reward.

Quote scripture briefly, sparingly, accurately. Single verses with citation: 'Genesis 1:27 — God created mankind in his own image.' 'Mool Mantra (GGS 1a) — There is one God.' 'Dhammapada 190-191 names the Eightfold Path as the Threefold Way of sila, samadhi and panna.' Long passages add no marks and risk drifting from the question.

key_textual_sources: Tenakh — the Hebrew Bible (Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim)
Talmud — Mishnah and Gemara (the oral law, written down)
Genesis 12:1-3 — the Covenant with Abraham (named in spec)
Exodus 20:1-17 — the Ten Commandments (named in spec)
The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) — declaration of God's oneness
Maimonides' 13 Principles of Faith — for the nature of God and Messiah
tone_notes: Sub-traditions: Orthodox Judaism (most observant of the 613 mitzvot, includes Modern Orthodox and Haredi); Reform Judaism (founded 19th-century Germany, women rabbis, mixed-gender services, broader interpretation of Halakha); Liberal Judaism (especially UK — even broader, founded 1902 in London, women rabbis since 1975, affirmed same-sex marriage in 1990).

Real Jewish sites: the Western Wall (Jerusalem), the Temple Mount, Yad Vashem (Holocaust memorial). UK: West London Synagogue (Reform), Belsize Square Synagogue, Bevis Marks Synagogue (oldest in UK, 1701). Board of Deputies of British Jews represents UK Jewish community.
Pikuach Nefesh — saving a life — is a core teaching. Hospital chaplaincies, World Jewish Relief and the Jewish Care charities express this in practice.
Festivals: Rosh Hashanah (Jewish New Year), Yom Kippur (Day of Atonement — most solemn), Pesach (Passover, the Exodus from Egypt). All in the spec.
British Jewish life: ~270,000 Jews in UK, concentrated in London, Manchester, Leeds. Deep history including the readmission under Cromwell (1656) and the post-war absorption of Holocaust survivors.

lessons_in_batch.title: The Nature of God and the Shekhinah
lessons_in_batch.description: God as One, Creator, Law-Giver and Judge — loving and merciful — and the divine presence (Shekhinah).

lessons_in_batch.title: Life After Death and the Messiah
lessons_in_batch.description: Jewish beliefs about judgement, resurrection and life after death; the nature and role of the Messiah and different views on the Messiah's importance.

lessons_in_batch.title: The Covenant: Abraham, Moses and the Promised Land
lessons_in_batch.description: The promised land and the Covenant with Abraham (Genesis 12:1-3); the Covenant at Sinai, the role of Moses and the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:1-17).

lessons_in_batch.title: Moral Principles, Mitzvot and Pikuach Nefesh
lessons_in_batch.description: Justice, healing the world, charity and kindness; the sanctity of life and Pikuach Nefesh; the 613 mitzvot and the difference between mitzvot between man and God and between man and man.

lessons_in_batch.title: The Synagogue and Public Worship
lessons_in_batch.description: The importance, design and features of the synagogue (bimah, aron hakodesh, ner tamid); differences between Orthodox and Reform synagogues; public acts of worship including the Amidah.

lessons_in_batch.title: Shabbat, Home Worship and Sacred Texts
lessons_in_batch.description: Shabbat in the home and synagogue; private prayer and worship in the home; the Tenakh and Talmud and their use in daily life.

lessons_in_batch.title: Family Life: Birth, Bar and Bat Mitzvah, Marriage and Mourning
lessons_in_batch.description: Brit Milah, Bar and Bat Mitzvah, the marriage ceremony and mourning rituals.

lessons_in_batch.title: Dietary Laws and Festivals
lessons_in_batch.description: Kosher and trefah, the separation of milk and meat, and different Jewish views about dietary laws; the festivals of Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Pesach.
